::: {.lead}
A small studio is making *Skyward Kite*, a mobile game about a young kite
maker. The level designers have built ten levels, and the jumps work. But the
first testers say: "Why should I care? Where am I going, and why?" The game
has mechanics, but no story yet. In lecture 1 you met story as one of the
four elements of a game. In this lesson you take a story apart into four
building blocks: **character**, **setting**, **conflict** and **structure**.
For each block you learn what it is and what it does for the player. Every
section ends with a short task on a game you play.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary story protagonist antagonist setting conflict stakes three-act-structure inciting-incident climax story-resolution story-beat interest-curve >}}

## 2.1 Who do we follow? Character and goal

The testers of *Skyward Kite* jump through the levels, but they do not know
*who* they are. A story always follows someone who **wants** something. A
**story** is a series of events in which a character wants something, meets
obstacles and changes the situation.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 2.1 — Protagonist and antagonist"}
The **protagonist** is the main character of a story: the story follows
their goal. The **antagonist** is the character or force that works against
that goal.
:::

A good protagonist has three things (@fig-character):

- a **goal**: what they want, clear enough to say in one sentence;
- a **weakness**: something that makes the goal hard for them, such as a
  fear or a bad habit;
- a **change**: at the end, they are a little different from the start.

![The character card of Lina, the protagonist of Skyward Kite.](images/character-card.png){#fig-character width=90%}

In a game, the protagonist is often the character that the player
controls. So the player takes the goal of the character as their own goal.
This is the job of character in the player experience: it gives the player
a reason to play. When the hero is in danger, the player feels it too.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 2.1 — The characters of Skyward Kite"}
1. **Protagonist:** Lina, a young kite maker. *Goal:* bring the wind back to
   her village. *Weakness:* she is afraid of heights.
2. **Antagonist:** Captain Gale, a sky pirate who keeps the wind in a giant
   glass jar to sell it.
3. **Change:** at the end, Lina climbs the highest tower without fear.
4. For the player: every jump in a level is now a step towards the jar, not
   just a jump.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Describing a character only by looks: "a girl with a red scarf." Looks help
the player remember a character, but they do not drive a story. Always
write the goal first: "a kite maker who wants to bring the wind back."
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · The protagonist of your game"}
Choose a game that you play on your phone (or a film you know well).

1. Write the name of the protagonist and their goal in one sentence.
2. Write one weakness, and one antagonist. If the game has none, write "none".

*Your result:* a small character card with four lines: name, goal, weakness,
antagonist.

::: {.check}
A good card looks like: "Name: Ali. Goal: win back his family's farm.
Weakness: he trusts the wrong people. Antagonist: the greedy mayor."
Check: The goal is one sentence: what the hero wants; The weakness makes the goal harder; An antagonist, or "none".
:::
:::

## 2.2 Where and when? The setting

The second complaint of the testers is: "The levels all look the same. Where
am I?" A story happens in a place and a time, and its world has rules.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 2.2 — Setting"}
The **setting** is the place and the time of a story, together with the
rules of its world.
:::

A setting answers three questions (@fig-setting):

| Question | Skyward Kite | What it gives the player |
|---|---|---|
| **Where?** | a village on windy hills, and a pirate tower in the clouds | places to explore, a goal to see from far away |
| **When?** | one year after the wind stopped | a reason why everything is quiet and sad |
| **Which rules?** | kites carry messages and seeds between villages; without wind, nothing flies | the main mechanic: Lina rides her kite on the last winds |

: The three parts of a setting. {#tbl-setting}

![The setting of Skyward Kite: the village, the hills and the pirate tower in the clouds.](images/setting.png){#fig-setting width=92%}

In games, the setting does more than in a book. The player walks *through*
it, so the setting becomes the levels. Its rules become the mechanics. And
its colours and sounds set the mood, which you met in lecture 1.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 2.2 — The setting tells the story"}
The first level of *Skyward Kite* shows the village.

1. Broken windmills stand still on the hills: **where**, and a sign that
   something is wrong.
2. Torn kites hang from the trees: **when**, a long time after the wind
   stopped.
3. A child sends a message by running, not by kite: a **rule** of the world
   no longer works.
4. The player understands the problem before anyone says a word.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Thinking that the setting is only a background picture. In a game the
setting has rules that change what the player can do. A "frozen kingdom"
where the ice is not slippery is only a picture, not a setting.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · The setting of your game"}
Use the same game.

1. Write three lines: **where**, **when**, and **one rule** of its world.
2. Add one sentence: how does one part of the setting change what the player
   can do?

*Your result:* four sentences about the setting.

::: {.check}
A good answer looks like: "Where: a city on the sea. When: after a great
flood. Rule: boats are the only way to travel. The rule changes play: the
player steers a boat instead of walking."
Check: Where, when and one rule of the world; One sentence on how the setting changes what the player can do.
:::
:::

## 2.3 What stands in the way? Conflict and stakes

A character with a goal and nothing in the way is boring: Lina walks to the
tower, opens the jar, the end. A story needs **conflict**.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 2.3 — Conflict and stakes"}
**Conflict** is the struggle between what a character wants and what stands
in the way. The **stakes** are what the character will lose if the goal is
not reached.
:::

A simple sentence holds the whole conflict: **"X wants Y, but Z."** Conflict
comes from three places (@fig-conflict):

- **another character**: an enemy, a rival (Captain Gale);
- **the world**: nature, a storm, a broken bridge, a cruel law;
- **the self**: a fear, a doubt, a bad choice from the past.

![Three sources of conflict for Lina.](images/conflict.png){#fig-conflict width=90%}

In games, conflict is where story and gameplay meet. The obstacles of the
story become the **challenges** of the levels. The stakes make the player
care about winning: losing a level is not only "game over", it is "the
village stays silent".

::: {.callout-note title="Example 2.3 — Lina's conflicts"}
1. The whole conflict: "Lina wants to bring the wind back, **but** Captain
   Gale keeps it in a jar in his tower."
2. Other character: Gale's crows attack Lina's kite in level 4.
3. World: the last winds are weak, so Lina must find warm air to rise.
4. Self: Lina is afraid of heights; the higher levels show a shaking screen
   when she looks down.
5. Stakes: without wind, the windmills cannot grind flour, and the village
   will have no bread by winter.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
A conflict without stakes. "Lina must reach the tower" is a task. "Lina must
reach the tower before winter, or the village will starve" is a conflict
with stakes. The stakes make the player hurry.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · The conflict of your game"}
Use the same game.

1. Write its conflict in one sentence: "X wants Y, but Z."
2. Name the source of the conflict (another character, the world or the
   self) and the stakes.

*Your result:* two sentences: the conflict, and its source and stakes.

::: {.check}
A good answer looks like: "The hero wants to save his sister, but the ice
queen locks her in a castle. Source: another character. Stakes: the sister
freezes by the full moon."
Check: The sentence has the form "X wants Y, but Z"; A source (another character, the world or the self) and the stakes.
:::
:::

## 2.4 Beginning, middle, end: the three-act structure

The designers now have a character, a setting and a conflict. In which order
should the events come? Most stories in films, books and games use the same
basic shape: the **three-act structure** (@fig-acts).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 2.4 — Three-act structure"}
The **three-act structure** builds a story in three parts. **Act 1** (the
setup) shows the normal world and ends with the **inciting incident**: the
event that starts the conflict. **Act 2** (the confrontation) brings bigger
and bigger obstacles. **Act 3** contains the **climax**, the moment of
highest tension, and the **resolution**, which shows the new situation.
:::

![The three-act structure. The tension rises through act 2 and is highest at the climax.](images/three-acts.png){#fig-acts width=94%}

Act 2 is usually the longest. In a game it holds most of the levels. Act 1
is often the tutorial: the player learns the controls while the world is
still safe.

Each important event of the story is a **story beat**: an event that
changes the situation, such as a new place, a new danger or a new piece of
information. A **tension curve** shows how tense each part of the story is.
In a good structure it starts with a strong moment, rises through act 2
with short calm rests, peaks at the climax, and falls in the resolution.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 2.4 — Skyward Kite in three acts"}
1. **Act 1 (setup):** Lina mends kites in the silent village (normal world).
   *Inciting incident:* one last kite falls from the sky with a map to
   Gale's tower.
2. **Act 2 (confrontation):** Lina flies across the hills, the forest of
   crows and the storm clouds. Each land is harder, and she must face her
   fear of heights.
3. **Act 3:** *Climax:* on top of the tower, Lina breaks the jar while Gale
   tries to stop her. *Resolution:* the wind returns, and the village holds
   its kite festival.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Putting the climax in the middle. If the biggest fight is in level 5 of 10,
the last levels feel empty. The tension must rise until near the end, then
fall quickly in the resolution.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Five events of a story"}
Use the same game, or a film you know well.

1. Write five events in order: the normal world, the inciting incident, a
   big obstacle, the climax, the resolution.
2. Mark which act each event belongs to.

*Your result:* a list of five events with their acts.

::: {.check}
A good answer looks like: "1. The hero lives on a quiet farm (act 1). 2. A
letter says that his sister is in danger: the inciting incident (act 1). 3.
He crosses the frozen mountains (act 2). 4. He fights the ice queen: the
climax (act 3). 5. The siblings return home (act 3, the resolution)."
Check: Five events in order; The climax is near the end, in act 3.
:::
:::

## Case study: Skyward Kite

*Skyward Kite* is a made-up mobile game. **Lina**, a young kite maker who is
afraid of heights, lives in a village on windy hills. One year ago, the sky
pirate **Captain Gale** stole the wind and locked it in a giant glass jar in
his tower in the clouds. Without wind, kites cannot carry messages, the
windmills stand still, and the village will have no bread by winter. One
day a last kite falls from the sky with a map to the tower. Lina flies
across the hills, the forest of crows and the storm clouds, breaks the jar
on top of the tower and brings the wind home. The Game challenge of the
interactive lesson uses this story. In the mini-game below, you sort the
pieces of the story into character, setting and conflict, and then put its
events into the three acts.

{{< sim file="sims/story-sorter.html" poster="sims/story-sorter.png" title="Story Sorter: the building blocks of Skyward Kite" kind="game" height="600" >}}

## Further reading

Schell, *The Art of Game Design*, 3rd ed., the chapters on story, on story
and game structures, and on the worlds in which games take place; McKee, *Story*,
HarperCollins, 1997, on character, conflict and structure (the inciting
incident and the climax).

## Exercises

1. What three things does a good protagonist have?
2. Why does a player care about the goal of the character they control?
3. Name the three parts of a setting, with one example of each from a game
   you know.
4. Explain with an example how a rule of the setting becomes a mechanic.
5. Write the conflict of a game you know as "X wants Y, but Z."
6. Name the three sources of conflict. Give one example of each.
7. What are stakes? Why do they make a game more exciting?
8. Put in order and name the act: the climax, the normal world, a big
   obstacle, the inciting incident, the resolution.
9. *Skyward Kite*: name the protagonist, the antagonist, the inciting
   incident and the climax.

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. A goal, a weakness, and a change at the end.
2. The player controls the character, so the player takes the character's goal as their own goal. When the character is in danger, the player feels it too.
3. Where, when and the rules of the world. For example: a city in the future (where), at night after a war (when), robots must obey humans (a rule).
4. For example: in Skyward Kite, "kites fly on the wind" is a rule of the world; it becomes the main mechanic, riding the kite on winds.
5. For example: "A fox wants to get home, but the bridge is out and the forest is dark."
6. Another character (a rival), the world (a storm), the self (a fear).
7. What the character will lose if the goal is not reached. They give the player a reason to hurry and to care about winning.
8. Normal world (act 1), inciting incident (end of act 1), big obstacle (act 2), climax (act 3), resolution (act 3).
9. Lina; Captain Gale; the last kite falls with a map to the tower; Lina breaks the jar on top of the tower while Gale tries to stop her.
:::
